episode_title: From Drude to Ballistic: Scattering Mechanisms in Two-Dimensional Electron Gases

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Welcome back to arXiv Morning, Nano and Correlated. This weekend we're prepping for lecture eight of Ihn's Semiconductor Nanostructures course at ETH, which is on Drude transport and scattering mechanisms. It's the lecture where the course stops treating mobility as a magic number you look up in a table and starts asking: what, microscopically, is slowing the electrons down, and how do we diagnose it from a transport measurement.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Which is honestly the question I always wanted answered properly. We throw around mobility in every quantum Hall paper, but half the time it's just quoted like a sample quality score. I want to know what's actually inside that number.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and that's the spirit of this lecture's reading list. Four papers, four completely different ways of attacking the same underlying question: what scatters electrons in a two-dimensional electron gas, and how far can you push transport before the simple classical picture breaks down. Let's build the classical picture first, quickly, because everything else is a variation on it.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Drude model. Electrons as classical particles, accelerated by a field, randomized by collisions after some average time tau.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right. You write the equation of motion for the drift velocity, add a damping term with a single relaxation time tau, and in steady state you get conductivity equals the carrier density times the elementary charge squared times tau, divided by the effective mass. Mobility is just that same tau times charge over effective mass. Two knobs: how many carriers you have, and how long they travel, on average, between randomizing collisions.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And mean free path is just the velocity at the Fermi surface times that time.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Yes, and for a textbook high-mobility GaAs two-dimensional electron gas at low temperature, that's a genuinely useful number to keep in your head. Mobility of order ten to a hundred square meters per volt-second, scattering times of tens of picoseconds, and mean free paths that can reach several microns. That's wild if you think about it: an electron sails in a straight line across a distance bigger than many lithographic features before it even notices an impurity.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Which is presumably why one of today's papers can even talk about ballistic transport through a micron-sized cross. But before we get there, what actually sets tau? It's not one mechanism, right?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: No, and this is the heart of the lecture. You have several independent scattering mechanisms operating at once: ionized impurity scattering, either from the background doping or from remote dopants set back in a modulation-doped barrier; interface or quantum-well-boundary roughness scattering; alloy disorder scattering if you're in a ternary compound; phonon scattering, which matters more as temperature rises; and, in multi-subband systems, intersubband scattering, where an electron doesn't just change momentum within one subband but jumps to a different subband altogether. Matthiessen's rule says you add up the scattering rates, one over tau, from each independent mechanism, to get the total rate.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the fastest mechanism wins, basically, since it's rates you add, not times.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, whichever channel is fastest dominates the total scattering rate. And there's one more subtlety that the lecture leans on hard, and that three of today's four papers use explicitly or implicitly: there are actually two different scattering times you can extract from the same two-dimensional electron gas, and they're not the same number.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Go on, because this always confused me a bit.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The transport scattering time, the one that sets the Drude mobility, weighs each collision by how much it changes your forward momentum, essentially a factor of one minus cosine of the scattering angle. A tiny-angle, forward-glancing collision barely randomizes your velocity, so it barely counts toward resistivity. But there's also a single-particle or quantum lifetime, which just counts how often you scatter at all, regardless of angle, because any scattering event dephases the quantum state and broadens the Landau levels you'd see in a magnetic field. You get that second number from the damping of Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations, the so-called Dingle factor.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So if your dominant scatterer is long-range and smooth, like a charged impurity sitting far away behind a spacer layer, it mostly nudges you a little, forward-biased collisions, so the transport time is long even though you're actually scattering quite often in the quantum sense.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Precisely. The ratio of transport time to quantum time becomes a fingerprint. A ratio close to one tells you scattering is isotropic, short range, like alloy disorder or a hard, nearby impurity. A ratio of tens tells you it's dominated by remote, long-range Coulomb scatterers that mostly forward-scatter. That one ratio, without any detailed modeling, tells you which physical mechanism is in charge. Keep that in your pocket, because paper one uses it directly.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Okay. So with that toolkit, Drude formula, Matthiessen's rule, and the transport-versus-quantum-time ratio, let's go to the papers. Which one first?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Let's go chronological, because it tells a nice story. We start in 1982, with Stormer, Gossard, and Wiegmann, paper eight point three, which is the first direct observation of intersubband scattering. Then 1996, Friedland and colleagues, paper eight point one, who engineer around remote impurity scattering with a genuinely clever trick. Then 1997, Geim and company, paper eight point two, who push a two-dimensional electron gas into the opposite limit, ballistic rather than diffusive, and turn that into a magnetometer. And we finish in 2012, with Weber, Simmons, and colleagues, paper eight point four, asking whether Ohm's law itself survives once your wire is only a few atoms wide.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: A nice arc: mechanisms, mitigation, the ballistic limit, and finally the atomic limit. Let's start with Stormer.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So, the setting. By the early eighties, two-dimensional electron systems were already a mature playground, mostly in silicon inversion layers at a metal-oxide-semiconductor interface. People understood, both from theory and experiment, that at low temperature two mechanisms dominated scattering: ionized impurities and interface roughness. But there was a third mechanism, predicted theoretically by Mori and Ando a couple of years earlier, that nobody had pinned down experimentally: scattering between two populated electric subbands.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Why would that even be a separate channel? Isn't it just more impurity scattering, now with more electrons around to do it?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Good question, and this is exactly the kind of thing to picture with Fermi circles. When you only occupy the lowest subband, every electron sits on one circle of radius k-F-one in momentum space, and ionized-impurity or roughness scattering just moves you around that same circle. Once a second subband starts filling, up to the Fermi level, there is now a second circle, smaller, of radius k-F-two, available at essentially the same energy. Suddenly an electron in the ground subband can scatter into a state on that second circle. That's a genuinely new relaxation channel, with a big available range of momentum transfer, that simply didn't exist before the second subband turned on.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the theoretical prediction was that mobility should drop suddenly, almost like a step function, exactly at the gate voltage or density where the second subband starts to fill.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right, an abrupt kink. The problem experimentally was finding a system where you could sweep smoothly and continuously through that threshold and resolve both subbands independently. Silicon inversion layers didn't give you that kind of clean, continuous control. So Stormer and colleagues turned to the then-new modulation-doped gallium arsenide, aluminum gallium arsenide heterojunction, which is essentially the system that gave birth to the whole high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas field.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, the classic structure: donors in the aluminum gallium arsenide barrier, electrons spilling across the interface into the undoped gallium arsenide, confined by their own Coulomb attraction to the ionized donors, forming the triangular potential well.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and the key extra ingredient here is a backside electrode, a copper plate glued to the substrate, used as a gate to continuously tune the electron density across the sample. Standard Hall bar geometry, measured at four point two kelvin, magnetic field normal to the plane, both Hall and Shubnikov-de Haas magnetoresistance recorded simultaneously as they swept the gate from strongly negative, which depletes the electron gas, up through zero to strongly positive, which populates more carriers.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the magnetoresistance traces are the smoking gun, I assume.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They are. At minus six hundred volts, the magnetoresistance shows one clean, single-period oscillation: one subband, one Fermi circle, one frequency in the oscillation as a function of inverse field. At plus two hundred volts the trace is visibly a superposition of two different periods, unambiguous evidence that a second, excited subband is now populated with its own, smaller, Fermi wavevector. Since each Shubnikov-de Haas frequency gives you a density, you literally read off the density in each subband separately just from the beat pattern.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So they've got density in each subband as a function of gate voltage. Where does the mobility drop show up?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: This is where it gets nice. They also measure the ordinary Hall density and Hall mobility as functions of gate voltage. In a simple one-carrier system, both would just track smoothly with density. Instead, both curves show a break, a kink, right at the gate voltage where the second subband switches on. The total Hall density actually dips below what you'd expect from a simple capacitor model, because now you have two types of carriers with different mobilities contributing to one Hall signal, and a two-carrier Hall measurement doesn't just average them, it weights them unequally.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, this is the classic two-channel Drude trick, isn't it: if you have two carrier species with densities n-one and n-two and mobilities mu-one and mu-two, the measured Hall density and Hall mobility are some nontrivial combination, and only if the mobilities are equal does the Hall density simply measure the total.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly right, and that's the equation they invert. Using the independently known subband densities from Shubnikov-de Haas, together with the measured Hall density and Hall mobility, they solve for the mobility of the ground subband and the mobility of the excited subband separately, across the whole transition region. That's the real result of the paper: not just a kink, but a complete, separated map of mu-one of n and mu-two of n.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And what do they find for the sizes?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The ground-subband mobility drops by about thirty percent right at the onset of the second subband, which they interpret directly as the fingerprint of intersubband scattering switching on. Theory at the time predicted a reduction by as much as a factor of three, so the measured effect is real but smaller than the crude prediction, and the transition is smooth over a narrow density range rather than a sharp step, which they attribute partly to a small density gradient across the sample and partly to the finite energetic width of the excited subband smearing out the threshold.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the excited subband's own mobility?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Much lower than the ground subband's, which is itself a nice and very physical result. Remember, the dominant scatterer here is the ionized donor sheet in the barrier, a long-range Coulomb potential. Long-range Coulomb scattering favors small momentum transfer, and whether a given scattering event is small-angle or not depends on how big the Fermi wavevector is relative to the characteristic momentum transfer of the potential. The excited subband has a smaller Fermi wavevector, so the same Coulomb potential looks relatively harsher, more large-angle, to those electrons, and they end up with a distinctly inferior mobility.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the same impurity does more damage to electrons in the subband with fewer, more exposed states near the Fermi surface. It's a nice, simple geometric statement, kind of like how scattering off a Coulomb potential affects small Fermi circles harder.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's the right intuition. And to close the loop, they even get a number out of the excited subband mobility: a scattering time around point seven times ten to the minus thirteen seconds, which through the uncertainty relation corresponds to a level broadening of about one millielectron-volt, and they check that this broadening, converted into a density through the two-dimensional density of states, is consistent with the width of the transition region they actually observe. It's a tight, self-consistent story.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So to summarize this one: it's the first direct experimental proof that occupying a second subband doesn't just add more conducting carriers, it opens a genuinely new scattering channel that degrades the mobility of the carriers you already had, and the size of the effect depends on how different the two subbands' Fermi wavevectors are.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and for our lecture it's the clean, foundational demonstration that Matthiessen's rule of simply summing independent one-particle scattering rates has to be generalized the moment your system has more than one conducting subband, because now the channels talk to each other.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Great, that sets up the mechanisms side nicely. Now let's go to the engineering side, Friedland and colleagues from 1996, paper eight point one.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: This one is a lovely, somewhat sneaky materials trick. Context first: by the mid-nineties, the dominant limitation on mobility in high-quality modulation-doped quantum wells was remote ionized impurity scattering, meaning scattering off the donors sitting in the barrier, at some setback distance from the channel. The standard fix, known for over a decade, is to simply push the donors further away with a thicker spacer layer. That smooths the Coulomb potential the electrons feel, because distance strongly suppresses the Fourier components of the potential at the large wavevectors that matter for scattering.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: But that costs you density, because the donors are now further from the channel, so less of their charge actually transfers across.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right, and conductivity is the product of density and mobility, so there's a real trade-off; push the spacer too far and you kill the very carrier density you need for high conductivity. There's also a second trap: if you instead try to raise density by just doping harder, you risk populating a second subband, which, as we just discussed with Stormer's paper, opens an entirely new scattering channel and tanks your mobility anyway. So the question going into this paper is: can you somehow decouple the two goals, get both high density and high mobility, without simply relying on the spacer-distance trade-off?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And their trick is this superlattice barrier with aluminum arsenide and gallium arsenide.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Yes, and the physics behind it is genuinely elegant. A short-period aluminum arsenide, gallium arsenide superlattice, built from very thin layers, has its lowest conduction-band state derived not from the usual gamma point of the band structure but from the X point of aluminum arsenide. X-point electrons have a much heavier effective mass, roughly a quarter of the free electron mass in-plane, and more than the free electron mass along the growth direction. The idea is to place the silicon delta-doping sheet inside this superlattice barrier, so that these heavy X electrons form right next to the dopant layer.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And a heavier mass means stronger screening, because screening strength scales with the density of states at the Fermi level, which for a given density goes up with effective mass.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, that's the key physical lever. These heavy X electrons sit extremely close to the ionized donors, their own effective Bohr radius is only a couple of nanometers, smaller than the typical spacing between randomly placed donor atoms, which is around eight or nine nanometers. So each X electron can comfortably localize right in a potential minimum created by the random donor arrangement, screening that particular fluctuation very effectively and very locally, precisely because its wavefunction is small and its mass is large. And because these X electrons are heavy, they're also intrinsically low mobility, so even though they carry charge, they barely conduct, and because they're localized in the random potential minima, they contribute essentially no parallel conduction channel to confuse the measurement.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So you get a layer of heavy, slow, localized electrons that act almost like a smoothing blanket over the random donor potential, while the light, fast, conventional electrons in the actual quantum well barely notice the donors anymore because the heavy electrons have already smoothed out the roughest part of the landscape.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's exactly the picture, and it's worth noting how different this is from the usual spacer trick. You are not pushing the dopants further away; you are leaving the dopants close, which keeps the carrier transfer efficient and the density high, and instead inserting an entirely separate, auxiliary species of carrier whose whole job is to screen, not to conduct.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What did they actually build and measure?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Molecular beam epitaxy on gallium arsenide substrates. A ten nanometer gallium arsenide quantum well, with barriers made of sixty periods of a four-monolayer aluminum arsenide, eight-monolayer gallium arsenide superlattice. Silicon delta-doping sheets sit inside that superlattice, on both sides of the well, set back by either fourteen or ten nanometers in their two samples. They do standard Hall-bar magnetotransport at point three three kelvin, with some devices gated so they can tune density continuously, plus capacitance-voltage measurements and photoluminescence, plus self-consistent Schrodinger-Poisson calculations to back up the interpretation.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the headline transport numbers?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Mobilities up to a hundred and twenty square meters per volt-second, with densities above one times ten to the sixteen per square meter, and crucially, all in a single occupied subband, confirmed by a single-frequency Shubnikov-de Haas oscillation persisting up to the highest gate voltages, with no sign of parallel conduction. That combination of density and mobility was genuinely record-setting for that period, especially the conductivity achieved at liquid nitrogen temperature, which they report as several times higher than anything previously reported in a two-dimensional electron gas at seventy-seven kelvin.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: But the mobility-versus-density curve is apparently the weird part.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It is. At lower densities, mobility rises with density following the textbook power law for remote impurity scattering, mobility proportional to density to some power between one point five and two. That's completely standard, expected behavior; more carriers screen the impurities better, in the ordinary Thomas-Fermi sense. But then, over a narrow density window, the mobility shoots up far faster, with an effective power-law exponent exceeding eight, before saturating at the maximum mobility. An exponent like that is basically impossible to explain with an ordinary random-impurity scattering model; something qualitatively different is turning on in that density window.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's where the extra screening channel kicks in, the X electrons.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right, and here's where that transport-time over quantum-time ratio we discussed earlier becomes the diagnostic tool. In the high-mobility regime, they compute this ratio from the measured mobility and the single-particle lifetime extracted from Shubnikov-de Haas damping, and they get values of thirty-five and forty-seven for their two samples. Those are large numbers, very characteristic of a scattering mechanism dominated by distant, smooth, forward-scattering Coulomb centers, that is, remote ionized impurity scattering, not some new short-range mechanism. And importantly, this ratio stays essentially constant with density, which tells them the character of the scattering mechanism hasn't changed, only its strength has been suppressed.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the scattering is still remote impurity scattering in nature, it's just that the effective potential fluctuation the gamma electrons feel has been made much smoother, consistent with extra screening rather than a different mechanism altogether.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly the conclusion. But they still needed independent evidence that these mysterious extra carriers actually exist, since transport alone can't directly see localized, non-conducting charge. That's where the capacitance-voltage measurements come in. They separate the total measured capacitance, which is sensitive to any rechargeable carriers in the whole structure, from a quantity they call the two-dimensional capacitance, which is specifically sensitive only to carriers in the high-mobility channel in the quantum well. Exactly in the gate-voltage window where the mobility jumps, the total capacitance rises while the two-dimensional-channel-specific capacitance vanishes, meaning there's extra charge being added somewhere outside the quantum well, right where the mobility anomaly happens.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Nice, that's a genuinely independent confirmation, not just curve-fitting the transport data.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And then they close the loop with their self-consistent Schrodinger-Poisson calculation and with photoluminescence. The calculation shows exactly the expected picture: gamma electrons sitting in the gallium arsenide well, far below the barrier edges in energy, and X electrons appearing right in the aluminum arsenide layer nearest to the doping sheet, split into two sublevels separated by about twenty millielectron-volts due to the internal electric field between the X and gamma charge distributions. The photoluminescence spectra show a double-peaked band in the type-two, indirect recombination region, with a peak separation that matches that predicted twenty millielectron-volt splitting almost exactly, which is as close to a direct spectroscopic fingerprint of these X electrons as you can get.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So to pull this together: the headline physics is that you can defeat remote ionized impurity scattering not by physically separating dopants from the channel, which costs you density, but by placing a second, heavy, intentionally low-mobility carrier species right where the disorder is worst, so it screens the randomness locally without ever contributing to the measured conductance.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's it exactly, and it's a wonderful illustration for this lecture of two separate lessons: first, that the mobility-versus-density power law is itself a diagnostic of scattering mechanism, with ordinary remote-impurity scattering giving an exponent around one and a half to two; and second, that the transport-time to quantum-time ratio is a quantitative, nearly model-independent way to identify whether you're dealing with small-angle, remote scattering or something else, without ever needing a microscopic calculation of the actual potential.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Good, let's move to the opposite extreme: Geim and collaborators, paper eight point two, ballistic Hall micromagnetometry.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: This one is a genuine change of regime, and it's a great way to see the edges of the Drude picture. Everything we've discussed so far assumed the diffusive limit: the electron's mean free path is much shorter than the size of your device, so locally, everywhere inside the sample, you have well-defined local equilibrium, and the classical Hall relation, Hall resistance equal to magnetic field over the product of density and charge, holds no matter what the geometry of your sample looks like.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Because in the diffusive limit, the Hall voltage just comes from the balance between the electric force and the Lorentz force on the drifting carriers, and that balance doesn't care about the shape of the wire.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly. But now flip the ratio: take an extremely clean two-dimensional electron gas, with such a long mean free path that it exceeds the size of your lithographically defined device. Now electrons don't scatter off bulk impurities inside the device at all; the only thing they scatter off is the edges, the geometric boundaries you etched. That's the ballistic regime, and the simple, geometry-independent Hall formula simply stops being exactly true. The Hall voltage now depends on the actual spatial distribution of the magnetic field inside the device and on the specific shape of the junction.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Which sounds like it should be a complication, a headache for anyone trying to use a Hall probe. But I take it the authors turned this into a feature.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They did, and the way they did it is lovely. In the ballistic regime, at low magnetic fields, where the cyclotron radius is still larger than the width of the cross junction, there's a clean, derivable relation: the Hall resistance is proportional to the average magnetic field inside the cross, divided by density times charge, with some geometric prefactor of order one that accounts for the exact corner shape of the junction. In words: the Hall probe literally measures the average of the magnetic field over a small, well-defined area, the flux through the cross junction, rather than the field at one point.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So it becomes a tiny fluxmeter.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly what they say themselves, that it behaves like a miniature analog of a SQUID, but using a semiclassical, ballistic two-dimensional electron gas instead of a superconducting loop, and with a far smaller effective detection loop. For their smallest devices the sensitive area is of order a tenth of a square micron.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What's the actual device, and why does it have to be a two-dimensional electron gas specifically, rather than a plain metal Hall probe?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The device is a gallium arsenide, aluminum gallium arsenide heterostructure with the two-dimensional electron gas buried sixty nanometers below the surface, patterned by two rounds of lithography into a multi-terminal wire carrying a whole set of Hall crosses in a row. On top of selected crosses, they deposit small magnetic or superconducting particles directly in the sensitive region, and they leave one cross bare, empty, to serve as a reference that just tracks the applied field. The particles are aluminum disks of various diameters, from roughly a fifth of a micron up to a micron, plus the smallest ferromagnetic nickel disks they could pattern, around a hundred nanometers.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And the reason it has to be a semiconductor two-dimensional electron gas, rather than, say, gold, is twofold. First, the Hall coefficient scales as one over the carrier density, and a two-dimensional electron gas has a much lower carrier density than a metal, so the same flux produces a much larger Hall signal. Second, and this is the crucial one for this lecture, you need extremely high mobility, which they quote as around three hundred thousand square centimeters per volt-second, which is simply what gives you a mean free path long enough to actually be ballistic across a micron-scale cross junction. Without the clean, high-mobility material, you'd be stuck in the diffusive regime and lose the clean flux-averaging relation entirely.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So this device is basically a direct, deliberate exploitation of exactly the opposite limit from what the first two papers were trying to achieve. They were fighting to minimize scattering so they could get a high conductivity device; here, that same minimal scattering is repurposed so that the device becomes ballistic and acts as a geometric flux probe.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Nicely put, and it's a great moment to recap the criterion that decides which regime you're in: compare the mean free path, velocity at the Fermi surface times scattering time, against the relevant device dimension. Long mean free path relative to the device means ballistic, dominated by boundary scattering and geometry; short mean free path relative to the device means diffusive, dominated by bulk scattering mechanisms and described well by the ordinary Drude formulas we built the whole lecture around.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Okay, so what did they actually measure with this flux probe?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They measured individual superconducting aluminum disks and individual ferromagnetic nickel disks, one particle at a time, which at the time was a genuinely new capability; previous Hall-probe magnetometry had only looked at macroscopic, ensemble samples. By comparing the Hall signal under a particle to the reference cross's Hall signal tracking the bare applied field, they extract an effective magnetization curve for that one, individual, submicron object: expulsion of flux below the superconducting transition for the aluminum disks, and a magnetization response for the nickel disk even up to liquid-nitrogen temperature, around sixty kelvin, as long as the two-dimensional electron gas transport stays ballistic at that temperature.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And what sets the sensitivity floor? I'd guess thermal, Johnson noise, since you still have a finite resistance even in the ballistic regime.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's right, the ballistic cross still has a resistance, of order a few ohms for their micron-wide probes, set by the geometric, boundary scattering plus the contact resistance, and that resistance still generates ordinary Johnson noise. They quote a field resolution of about a ten-thousandth of a gauss per root hertz at liquid-nitrogen temperature, which translates into a magnetic-moment sensitivity of order a thousand Bohr magnetons, and they explicitly flag single-electron-spin detection as the eventual target if the probe design is optimized further.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So, to recap this one: by building a two-dimensional electron gas so clean that the mean free path outgrows the device, the Hall effect stops being the familiar bulk, geometry-independent effect from the Drude picture and becomes instead a direct, quantitative probe of the magnetic flux through a tiny, lithographically defined area, which they then use as a nanoscale magnetometer for individual superconducting and ferromagnetic particles.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and for the lecture, it's the perfect counterexample that sharpens the boundary of validity of everything we've said about Drude transport: the whole classical machinery assumes diffusive transport, and this paper lives right on the other side of that boundary, on purpose.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Great, last one: Weber, Simmons, and colleagues, Ohm's law surviving to the atomic scale, paper eight point four.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: This is the natural question to end on: does the entire Drude, Ohmic framework we've built even survive once the wire itself is only a handful of atoms wide? The context is classical downscaling of silicon electronics, where interconnects and leads eventually become comparable in size to the active devices themselves, and specifically, in the emerging field sometimes called solotronics, where a single dopant atom can define a functional device, you still need wires and leads to actually address that single dopant, and those leads have to be comparably tiny.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the worry is presumably surface and interface effects, since a wire a few nanometers wide has almost all its volume near a surface.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and there was already clear prior evidence of exactly that problem, in vapor-liquid-solid grown silicon nanowires, where resistivity shoots up exponentially once the diameter drops below about ten nanometers. The explanation proposed for that was a dielectric mismatch between the silicon wire and its surrounding environment, which raises the ionization energy of the dopants near the surface, so fewer dopants actually contribute a free carrier, and the wire effectively loses carriers as it gets thinner, on top of ordinary surface-roughness scattering.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So the question going into this paper is whether that resistivity blow-up is a fundamental, unavoidable law of nanowires, or whether it's an artifact of how those particular wires were grown.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right, and their answer is the latter, and they prove it with an extraordinarily precise fabrication technique. They use scanning tunneling microscope lithography on a hydrogen-terminated silicon surface: the STM tip locally desorbs the hydrogen resist along a chosen line, exposing bare silicon dangling bonds only there, down to a width of just two atomic dimer rows, about one and a half nanometers, and one atomic layer tall. Then they expose the surface to phosphine gas, which deposits phosphorus dopant atoms, but only onto the exposed dangling-bond regions, giving atomically precise, atomically abrupt doping purely within the written pattern. After that they grow a silicon overlayer by molecular beam epitaxy, which buries the doped wire fully inside bulk crystalline silicon, eliminating the surface and the dielectric mismatch entirely, since now the wire's environment is simply more silicon.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the doping density they achieve is apparently extreme.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Genuinely extreme: about a quarter of a monolayer of phosphorus within the written lines, corresponding in three dimensions to roughly ten to the twenty-one per cubic centimeter, which is about three orders of magnitude above the Mott metal-insulator transition density for phosphorus in silicon. The average spacing between dopant atoms ends up below one nanometer, smaller than the Bohr radius of an isolated phosphorus donor, about two and a half nanometers. That overlap is the whole point: individual donor wavefunctions overlap so strongly that the dopants can't behave as isolated, localized, weakly-ionized centers; they're forced into a genuinely metallic, fully ionized state.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So this sidesteps the dopant-deactivation mechanism from the start, by brute-force doping density, combined with removing the dielectric mismatch by embedding the wire in identical silicon on all sides.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly the two-pronged fix. They fabricate and measure five wires with different lithographic widths, from about eleven nanometers down to one and a half nanometers, and lengths from tens to a few hundred nanometers, all showing clean, linear, ohmic current-voltage behavior at four point two kelvin, with current densities up to five times ten to the five amperes per square centimeter, which is approaching the current-carrying capability of state-of-the-art copper interconnects. That alone is a striking practical result for a doped silicon wire a few atoms wide.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: But the real test of Ohm's law is whether resistivity stays constant as you shrink the wire, independent of its cross-section, right? Otherwise it's not really Ohm's law surviving, it's just a low resistance.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and that's their key figure. They don't just use the lithographic width to compute resistivity; they use atomistic tight-binding simulations, with a code called NEMO-3D, to calculate the actual electronic charge distribution, which spreads out somewhat beyond the lithographic pattern into the surrounding silicon, following roughly an exponential decay analogous to a donor wavefunction. From that they extract an effective electronic cross-sectional area and an effective electronic diameter for each wire, which turns out to be noticeably larger than the lithographic width, especially for the narrowest wires.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And once you use that physically meaningful area instead of just the lithographic width, what happens to the resistivity?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It stays essentially flat. Across nearly two decades of effective diameter, down to about two point three nanometers for their narrowest wire, the resistivity sits at an average around point three milliohm centimeters, with a minimum as low as point one milliohm centimeter for one sample, both consistent with the resistivity of bulk silicon doped to the same density. That's the headline: no exponential blow-up, no diameter dependence, in sharp contrast with the vapor-liquid-solid-grown wires, which do show that exponential rise once you go below ten nanometers even after people tried to correct for surface depletion effects.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So Ohm's law, in the sense of a constant, size-independent resistivity, really does survive, as long as you remove the two things that were secretly breaking it before: incomplete ionization from dielectric mismatch, and insufficient doping density.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's the conclusion, and they go one step further to connect this classical Drude picture with the mesoscopic, mode-counting picture you've already met in this course. They use their tight-binding band structure to count how many conducting modes exist at the Fermi energy in these wires, and remarkably it saturates at six modes even in the narrowest wire, and even in the idealized limit of a single, one-atom-wide chain of dopants, simply because silicon has six equivalent conduction-band valleys and each valley contributes its own conducting channel.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That sounds like a Landauer-style calculation, counting modes and adding a quantized contact resistance, rather than a purely classical Drude calculation.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: It is, and that's exactly the beautiful bridge this paper draws. They compute the expected resistance using a formula that looks like the Landauer multimode resistance, Planck's constant over twice the electron charge squared times the number of modes, multiplying a factor of one plus the wire length over the elastic mean free path. The first part is the quantized, ballistic contact resistance set purely by mode counting; the second part is exactly the familiar diffusive, Ohmic term, resistance growing linearly with length, divided by a mean free path they take from independent measurements of similarly doped systems, around eight nanometers.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And because their wires are tens to hundreds of nanometers long, much longer than that eight nanometer mean free path, the diffusive term dominates heavily over the ballistic contact term.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, which is why, even though the cross-section is atomic, the overall transport is still safely in the diffusive, Drude-like, Ohmic regime, length scaling linearly, resistivity independent of cross-section, rather than the ballistic, Landauer-dominated regime we just saw exploited on purpose in the Geim paper. And when they plug in the mode count and the mean free path, the calculated resistances land close to the measured ones for every single wire, within experimental scatter.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So this paper is almost a unifying statement for the whole lecture: Drude transport, built on mean free path and scattering mechanisms, isn't a low-resolution approximation that quantum mechanics eventually erases as you shrink a device; it's a limit that survives down to the atomic scale as long as the ratio of wire length to mean free path stays large, and the quantum, mode-counting physics only shows up as a prefactor, through the number of conducting channels.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's a great way to put it, and it's also a very practical result: it tells device engineers, and quantum-computing architects using single dopants, that they can realistically scale their wiring down to the atomic limit and still get metallic, Ohmic, low-resistivity leads, as long as they control doping density and avoid dielectric mismatch, exactly the scattering-mechanism bookkeeping this whole lecture is about.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Let's pull the whole episode together, then, because these four papers really do form a coherent arc around one lecture.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They do. Start with the basic Drude picture: conductivity set by density and a single scattering time, but that single time is secretly an average over several independent, additive mechanisms, and even that addition rule has to be generalized once more than one subband is occupied. Stormer's 1982 paper gives you the first clean, quantitative proof that a second occupied subband doesn't just add carriers, it opens a brand-new scattering channel that specifically degrades the mobility you already had, and shows you how to disentangle two coexisting carrier species using nothing more than the two-carrier Hall formula.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Then Friedland's 1996 paper shows you can actively fight the dominant remote-impurity scattering mechanism, not by brute-force spacer engineering, which trades off density for mobility, but by adding an auxiliary, heavy, intentionally non-conducting carrier species that screens the random dopant potential locally, right where it's needed, and the diagnostic tools for proving that, the mobility-density power law and the transport-time over quantum-time ratio, are exactly the scattering-mechanism toolkit from the lecture.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Then Geim's 1997 paper shows you the other edge of the whole framework: push mobility, and therefore mean free path, high enough relative to your device size, and the ordinary, geometry-independent Drude Hall effect stops applying altogether, and you enter a ballistic regime where the Hall probe becomes a literal, quantitative flux meter, sensitive enough to weigh the magnetization of a single submicron magnetic particle.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And Weber's 2012 paper closes the loop by asking the question in the opposite direction: shrink the wire itself down to a few atoms wide, and ask whether Ohm's law, constant resistivity independent of size, survives. It does, as long as you keep the wire doped densely and uniformly enough, and embedded in a dielectrically matched environment, and as long as the wire length still vastly exceeds the elastic mean free path, so you remain safely in the diffusive, Drude-like regime, with the quantum mode-counting physics only entering as a well-defined prefactor.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Which, for anyone heading into Thursday's lecture, is really the whole point of studying Drude transport and scattering mechanisms properly: it's not a toy model you outgrow, it's a remarkably durable framework, and knowing how to diagnose which mechanism dominates, from a mobility-density power law, from a transport-time to quantum-time ratio, from a kink at a subband threshold, or from how resistivity does or doesn't scale with size, is a genuinely transferable skill you'll use again and again, well beyond gallium arsenide quantum wells.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That's a good place to stop. See everyone Thursday for lecture eight, and good luck to whoever's presenting these papers in the exercise class.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Thanks for listening, and we'll see you next weekend for the next installment of arXiv Morning.
